text.normalisation.label: GeCON "is insensitive to normalization of data" (Methods, advantage iv)

cause.summary: Eq. (5) applies atan2 to the two raw values, so the angle depends on their ratio, not their difference. On Yeast KY's log values (around 7) almost every angle sits near 45 or 135 degrees and GeCON connects all 27,966 pairs; on the site's normalised version of the same genes it connects 1,226 (tau 20, theta 0.6). 97% of the log data's angles lie within 5 degrees of 45 or 135.

table2.summary: GeCON as the paper describes it ranks pairs no better than chance on these data (mean AUPR 0.203, the share of true pairs is 0.203; mean AUROC 0.485), while minet's methods reach AUPR 0.275 to 0.291 and AUROC 0.535 to 0.61. At theta 0.5 and tau 20 it connects 84% to 100% of all pairs, because on positive values almost every edge angle of Eq. (5) sits near 45 or 135 degrees. No variant we tried brings GeCON's mean scores near the paper's (best mean AUPR 0.255 against 0.633); the few single cells that fall within printed precision are not counted as agreement. The comparators' values differ too, so the authors' simulations and scoring cannot be recovered.

page.lede: In 2014 Roy, Bhattacharyya and Kalita built co-expression networks from the angles between neighbouring expression values. Their Java program is gone. We rebuilt it from the equations and reran the paper. Of {items} results, {exact} came back exactly, {agrees} agree, {partly} partly agree and {differs} differ; {not_attempted} were not attempted.
page.items_caption: Every figure, table and claim of the paper, with our value and the verdict computed from it.
page.claims_line: The paper's main claim does not hold on our run. GeCON, built as the paper describes it, ranks gene pairs no better than chance on the DREAM data, and the best of ARACNE, CLR and MRNET beats it on 12 of 13 datasets in every score. The likely reason is in Eq. (5): on positive data almost every edge angle sits near 45 or 135 degrees, so almost every pair is connected. Why the paper's scores are so much higher is open.
came_back: GeCON as the Python package gecon, from Eqs. (4) to (11). Fig. 7's worked example comes back exactly: 138 and 52 degrees.
Both profile plots came back from public data, value for value: GEO GDS3702 and Cheng and Church's yeast matrix.
The bars draw Table 2. 152 of the 153 visible bars sit within 0.01 of the table; D13's CLR AUROC bar stands at 0.53, the table says 0.51.
All 13 datasets of Table 1. D9 to D13 are the DREAM4 release; D1 to D8 we simulated with a Python port of GeneNetWeaver, checked against that release.
GeCON is faster than ARACNE at every size, 15 times at 3000 genes on our machine.
The yeast ribosome and DNA replication modules came back; 7 of 17 terms we could test were found.
buried: Table 2: GeCON's scores. Ours are near chance; the paper's mean AUPR is about three times ours (0.633 against 0.203).
The authors' simulated DREAM3 data, their theta and tau per dataset, and how they scored a thresholded network.
The yeast sporulation file (it would not download) and the 517 gene Arabidopsis matrix (never found).
GeneMANIA's 2014 data and FuncAssociate, which gave Tables 4 and 5 their numbers.
Fig. 6, which shows modules the paper does not name.
page.matched_intro: What came back the same, and how we know.

page.closing: We dug GeCON back up in November 2026. It runs, it is fast, and on its own benchmark it does no better than chance.
